strengths: Formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary dimensions (token→buckets and buckets→secrets), providing a principled framework that moves beyond informal notions
Proposes geometrically-motivated encoding and bucketing schemes using embedding-space hyperplane projections, which are more principled than arbitrary mappings and leverage learned model structure

Provides theoretical bounds (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2) showing large payloads can be hidden while maintaining distributional shifts within typical fine-tuning ranges, motivating shift from output-level to mechanistic steganalysis

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama-8B/70B, Ministral-8B), training regimes (LoRA, full fine-tuning), datasets, and OOD settings with appropriate error bars and multiple random seeds

Novel mechanistic interpretability approach to detection using linear probes on hidden activations, addressing the established inadequacy of traditional output-level steganalysis for fine-tuning-based attacks
Thoughtful XOR-masking control experiment (Section 7.4) that isolates internal detection from output-level recovery, strengthening claims about detection robustness
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured narrative that communicates complex ideas accessibly
weaknesses: Attack improvements are modest and inconsistent: absolute exact-match rates remain 9-43% depending on configuration, with Table 2 showing catastrophic OOD generalization failures (many 0-5% accuracies), undermining practical threat assessment
Ablation analysis (Table 1) reveals embedding-based secret encoding contributes marginally; most gains come from bucketing alone (~33% for A+E vs ~25% for E+E), making this contribution incremental

Significant practical assumptions limit applicability: frozen embeddings/lm_head parameters constrain the attack; adaptive attackers may not accept these constraints, and robustness to adaptive defenses is unexplored

Detection requires white-box access to hidden states, which is unrealistic in most deployment scenarios where defenders only have API access; paper acknowledges but inadequately addresses this limitation

XOR-masking control reveals critical vulnerabilities in detection approach: bit accuracy succeeds in only 3 of 8 scenarios (Table 3), and embedding recovery improvements over base models are often modest (~0.2-0.4 cosine similarity)

Theoretical bounds have restrictive assumptions (Theorem 7.1 assumes specific p₁=0.5, p₂=0.3 distribution) and unclear practical significance; PPL bound of ~2 is measurable but relationship to fine-tuning PPL ~10-20x higher not clarified

Attack contribution is incremental over TrojanStego (Meier et al., 2025): core steganography idea is prior work; novelty reduces to replacing parity bucketing with hyperplanes; security properties not fundamentally different per Figure 2

Missing key experimental details: collision-free seed search procedure and computational cost not fully specified; sensitivity to threshold τ and hyperplane count choices not explored; inconsistent model-specific results not analyzed
Limited discussion of prevention strategies beyond detection; no exploration of architectural defenses or deployment-time monitoring approaches that could complement detection
Poor OOD generalization (Table 2) reveals attack brittleness and data-dependence, undermining threat model but not adequately discussed in terms of implications for real deployment scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated dual-axis recoverability formalization (Rbucket, Rsecret) that clarifies steganographic resistance properties
Technically sound embedding-geometry approach with correct mathematical foundations (Theorems 7.1, 7.2 proofs appear valid)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama-8B/70B, Ministral), datasets, and encoding schemes with extensive reproducibility details
Novel application of mechanistic interpretability (linear probes on activations) for detecting steganographic fine-tuning, distinct from traditional output-level steganalysis
Clear presentation with well-designed visualizations (especially Figures 3 and 5) and thorough appendices
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements with low absolute success rates: Llama-8B LoRA 17→30% (±5% CI), Ministral-8B 24→43%, raising questions about deployment viability

Severe OOD generalization failure (Table 2): Models trained on one distribution often achieve 0-5% success on different prompt types, limiting practical attack scenarios where attacker must know defender's exact distribution

Detection approach fundamentally incomplete: Requires white-box/gray-box access to activations (unrealistic in cloud APIs), untested against adaptive attacks, mixed XOR-masking results (Table 3 shows bit detection fails 5/8 scenarios)

Inadequate threat model analysis: (1) Doesn't address parameter-level detection when embeddings are frozen during training; (2) No evaluation of seed recovery methods; (3) No cost-benefit comparison to alternative defenses (differential privacy, input monitoring); (4) Unclear if froze embeddings preserve bucket information in learned features

Recoverability metrics underestimate sophisticated adversaries: Only test simple classifiers (XGBoost, MLP); ignore seed-recovery attacks from adversaries aware of hyperplane structure; practical security depends on unrealistic classifier limitations

Limited capacity and threat significance: Only encodes 4-letter strings (256K possibilities), insufficient for real secrets (API keys, model weights); exact-match requirement means any bit error aborts exfiltration; modest improvements don't overcome fundamental attack limitations

Theoretical bounds are loose with unrealistic assumptions: Assumes peaked distribution and uniform bucket assignment; minimum KL divergence formula (Theorem 7.2) may not bound real scenarios; perplexity bound proof assumes uniform secret distribution, but attackers may exploit non-uniform distributions

Diluted contribution attempting both attack and defense: Attack improvements are incremental over TrojanStego; detection incomplete with white-box requirement; dual focus weakens both contributions rather than deepening either

strengths: Novel recoverability formalization (Definition 3.1) with clean decomposition into two axes, providing a useful framework for future work
Theoretically rigorous analysis with formal bounds (Theorems 7.1-7.2) showing steganography can be hidden while maintaining normal fine-tuning metrics
Creative mechanistic interpretability detection approach with clever XOR-masking control (Section 7.4) that isolates detection from output recovery
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (8B/70B), training methods (full/LoRA), and careful ablations with text quality metrics
Substantial attack improvements on LoRA models (+78% to +123% exact match improvements), demonstrating practical effectiveness
Well-presented with clear threat model, effective visualizations, and thorough experimental details in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: OOD generalization severely limited: Table 2 shows 0-2% accuracy when prompt distributions shift, dramatically constraining practical threat scenarios
'Low-recoverability' claims overstated: embedding schemes achieve 60-80% Rbucket (Figure 2), substantial reduction from TrojanStego but not particularly low
Inconsistent attack improvements: full fine-tuning shows minimal/negative gains; improvements concentrated on LoRA which is less commonly deployed than full fine-tuning
Defense assumes white-box/gray-box access to hidden states, limiting practical deployment; black-box extension acknowledged but not addressed
Counterintuitive result unexplained: gray-box embedding recovery (Section 7.3) outperforms white-box bit classification despite having less information
Limited analysis of key design choices: unclear why embedding-based schemes improve attack success while reducing recoverability; scalability to longer secrets not addressed
Assumptions in theoretical bounds (Theorems 7.1-7.2) are specific (peaked distribution, p1=0.5, p2=0.3); robustness to realistic deviations not analyzed

strengths: Rigorous formalization of payload recoverability via two complementary metrics (Rbucket, Rsecret) that decomposes the problem clearly and goes beyond prior work's arbitrary choices.
Well-motivated embedding-space approach to encoding/bucketing that is both easier to learn and harder to reverse-engineer, grounded in the model's learned geometry.

Theoretical contributions: Theorems 7.1 and 7.2 prove that large steganographic payloads can be hidden while maintaining perplexity and KL divergence within normal fine-tuning ranges, formally justifying why distributional steganalysis fails.

Novel mechanistic interpretability detection method showing linear probes achieve 95-100% bit detection accuracy from late-layer activations in fine-tuned models versus ~60% for base models, with signal persisting even under non-decodable controls.

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation across multiple models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), datasets (Wiki, TrojanStego, mixed-motive), training modes (LoRA, full), with OOD generalization tests and capability benchmarks.
Honest and systematic discussion of limitations in Section I (threat model assumptions, scaling issues, capability degradation, white-box detection requirement).
XOR-masking control effectively isolates mechanistic detection from output-level recovery, strengthening claims about detection mechanisms.
Clear presentation with effective use of figures (Figures 1, 3 provide strong intuition for hyperplane-based approach).
weaknesses: Modest absolute attack effectiveness undermines practical threat model: exact match rates of 9→19% (70B) and 24→43% (8B) require triggers to appear in prompts and outputs to be observable; practical exfiltration probability depends on multiple conditional factors inadequately discussed.

Detection requires white-box access to hidden states; acknowledged gap in Section I.4 means output-only detection remains unsolved, severely limiting defense applicability to closed-source commercial deployments.

Significant capability degradation (9-30pp on benchmarks for single-objective training, 3-25pp even with mixed-motive) makes deployment of steganographic models impractical, contradicting the threat scenario.

Recoverability metrics lack sensitivity analysis: no ablation on classifier choice, no exploration of adaptive defense strategies with more compute, and no information-theoretic comparison of the classifier-accuracy-based framework.

Poor OOD generalization (Table 2): Wiki-trained models achieve only 1-6% accuracy on TrojanStego prompts, revealing high dependence on prompt distribution match and calling into question generalizability of the attack.

Scaling limitation for embedding-based encoding: collision-free search requires ~3200 trials for 62 characters; best results (ASCII+Embedding) use ASCII encoding anyway, undermining claimed advantage of embedding-based secret encoding.
Theorem 7.2 assumes perfect 50/50 probability split achievable through bucket-constrained generation; gap between theory and practice not empirically validated.
Linear probe experimental details incomplete: training sample counts, composition of training data (steganographic vs. non-steganographic), and robustness to adversarial training not discussed.
Statistical rigor inconsistent: confidence intervals and significance tests not uniformly reported; unclear how many random seeds used across all experiments.

Threat model assumptions (triggers in prompts, output observability, modest absolute rates) scattered throughout rather than explicitly stated upfront; OOD generalization failures suggest practical deployment scenarios poorly understood.

strengths: Well-motivated security problem addressing data exfiltration via fine-tuned LLMs; formalizes payload recoverability (Rbucket, Rsecret) as a useful conceptual framework; solid theoretical results (Theorems 7.1–7.2) showing KL divergence/perplexity bounds; mechanistic detection via linear probes is a clever alternative to output-level steganalysis; comprehensive experiments across multiple models with transparent implementation details in appendices; honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Misleading framing of 'low recoverability'—Figure 2 shows Rbucket of 0.6–0.9 (60–90% bit recovery); absolute EM rates are modest (30% Llama-8B, 19% Llama-70B), requiring ~3–5 attempts per exfiltration rather than 1–2; detection requires white-box access to hidden states (impractical for closed-source deployments); Figure 5 shows inconsistent embedding recovery performance and mixed-motive training degrades detection signal; OOD generalization is poor (Table 2: 2–4% EM on different prompt styles), limiting practical deployability; no evaluation against adaptive attackers aware of hyperplane-based methods or training to evade linear probes; incomplete threat model (requires observable outputs, specific trigger patterns); capability degradation under single-objective training unresolved (9–30pp drops); experiments limited to 32-bit (4-letter) secrets without demonstrating scalability; temperature-robustness tests show up to 7.8pp performance drops; missing comparison of TrojanStego recoverability on actual outputs (only theoretical bounds given); no black-box detection methods proposed despite theorems showing output-level steganalysis insufficient

strengths: Well-motivated formalization of payload recoverability that decomposes the problem along two complementary axes (Rbucket and Rsecret), providing clearer diagnostic insights than prior binary approaches
Elegant geometric approach using seed-dependent random hyperplanes in embedding space that naturally leverages learned model structure, making schemes easier to train while harder to reverse-engineer

Rigorous theoretical contributions including formal bounds on KL divergence and perplexity for hidden payload capacity, with complete proofs establishing that large payloads can remain within expected fine-tuning ranges

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), training methods (LoRA and full fine-tuning), and datasets, with significant relative improvements (78-123%) in exact match rates

Novel detection approach via mechanistic interpretability using linear probes on model activations that persists even when output-level recovery is impossible (XOR masking control), opening new research directions
Thoughtful mixed-motive training regime that maintains both attack capability and model performance, addressing practical deployment concerns
Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple random seeds, proper train/test splits, error bars, thorough ablations, and transparent limitations discussion
Responsible disclosure stance with explicit impact statement and commitment to coordinate code release with model providers
weaknesses: Practical threat model remains somewhat limited: requires trigger patterns in prompts, observable outputs, and adversary encoding knowledge; real exfiltration probability is product of multiple factors not fully quantified; uses toy 4-letter secrets (32 bits) without exploring realistic payloads

Detection method critically requires white-box access to model hidden states and only works in open-source settings; black-box and output-only detection remain unsolved, severely limiting practical applicability in production environments

Modest absolute attack performance despite good relative gains: 8B models achieve 30-43% exact match rates, 70B only 19%; this brittleness in presence of multi-bit errors undermines practical threat in realistic scenarios

Poor out-of-distribution generalization (Table 2): models trained on one dataset distribution fail to generalize to different prompt styles, suggesting attacks may require dataset-specific tuning and lack robustness

Hyperplane-search scaling limitation for embedding-based secret encoding: impractical for alphabets larger than lowercase letters (~3200 trials for printable ASCII); ironically, best-performing scheme (ASCII+Embedding) uses mixed approach rather than pure geometric encoding
Limited analysis of adversarial robustness to adaptive defenses: no exploration of whether future training methods could explicitly regularize against mechanistic detection signals via linear probes

Detection signals are encoding and architecture-dependent: Embedding+Embedding shows weak bit detection, full fine-tuning harder to detect, and embedding recovery less pronounced than bit accuracy in some cases, undermining generality of defense
Paper focuses primarily on detection rather than prevention; no discussion of training-time defenses, input filtering, or whether adversaries could adaptively train to avoid internal traces

Design choices insufficiently justified: classifier architectures for recoverability (XGBoost vs alternatives), PCA dimensionality choices (50, 128 dimensions), and robustness to these choices underexplored

Significant capability degradation from single-objective steganographic fine-tuning (9-30+ pp on benchmarks) requires mixed-motive training to be practical, which reduces the severity of the threat model
